concepts.title: Fibre to Fabric: Classification of Fibres

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Fibre to Fabric: Classification of Fibres' refers to.
questions.a: Every fabric begins as a fibre. Fibres classify into natural -- cotton, wool, silk, jute from plants and animals -- and man-made, further split into regenerated fibres like rayon and fully synthetic ones like polyester and nylon. Fibre properties decide what the finished cloth can do.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fibre to Fabric: Classification of Fibres'.
questions.a: Know the fibre, predict the fabric -- cotton breathes, wool warms, synthetics crease-resist.

concepts.title: Yarns and Fabric Construction: Weaving and Knitting

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Yarns and Fabric Construction: Weaving and Knitting' refers to.
questions.a: Fibres are spun into yarns, and yarns become fabric by two main routes: weaving, where lengthwise and crosswise yarns interlace at right angles, and knitting, where loops interlock. Woven cloth is stable and holds shape; knitted cloth stretches and yields.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Yarns and Fabric Construction: Weaving and Knitting'.
questions.a: Interlaced yarns give stable cloth; interlocked loops give stretch -- construction is destiny for fabric.

concepts.title: Finishes and Fabric Selection for Use

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Finishes and Fabric Selection for Use' refers to.
questions.a: Finishes alter fabric to fit its purpose -- bleaching, dyeing, printing for looks; starching, waterproofing, crease-resisting for performance. Selection means matching fibre, construction and finish to the end use, the wearer and the care the fabric can receive.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Finishes and Fabric Selection for Use'.
questions.a: Finishes dress the fabric for its job -- choose fibre, construction and finish together, not singly.
